# **Motivation**
***

Lupus is an {{< glossary "Autoimmune disease" display="autoimmune disease" >}} in which the body mounts an immune response against its own tissues [@niams_lupus_overview]. The @lfa2025lupusFacts estimates that 1.5 million Americans live with some form of the disease. While lupus can affect anyone, some populations are more affected than others.

In this case study, we will focus on {{< glossary "Systemic lupus erythematosus" display="systemic lupus erythematosus" >}} (SLE), the most common type, accounting for approximately 70% of lupus cases [@lfa2025lupusFacts]. SLE can be challenging to study because the affected tissues and experienced symptoms can vary strikingly between individuals and over time [@niams_lupus_overview]. The {{< glossary "Gene expression profile" display="gene expression profiles" >}} of blood immune cells provide an accessible window into some aspects of the immune activity associated with SLE [@catalina2019interferonSLE]. However, gene expression within a cell may reflect several overlapping influences:

- The cell's type and the functions it performs ({{< glossary "Immune-cell identity" display="cell identity" >}}).
- The cell's response to {{< glossary "Immune signaling" display="immune signaling" >}}.
- Differences between individuals, including differences in SLE severity [@kang2018multiplexed].

Latent variable analysis offers one way to investigate this complexity. A {{< glossary "Latent variable" display="latent variable" >}} is a feature that we do not measure directly but infer from observed data [@johnson2023cogapsWorkflow]. In this case study, we will use {{< glossary "CoGAPS" >}} to investigate how blood immune cells respond to {{< glossary "IFN-beta" display="interferon-beta" >}} (IFN-beta), an immune system signaling protein [@catalina2019interferonSLE]. We will compare {{< glossary "Gene expression" display="gene expression" >}} in IFN-beta-stimulated and untreated cells from the same {{< glossary "Donor" display="donors" >}} [@kang2018multiplexed]. These measurements show the expression of individual genes, but they do not directly separate the overlapping influences of cell identity and stimulation. CoGAPS looks for patterns across many genes and estimates how strongly each pattern is represented in each cell [@johnson2023cogapsWorkflow]. This helps us investigate a response shared across cell types alongside patterns associated with cell identity.

```{r}

The conditions contain different cells from the same donors; the diagrams are conceptual, not fitted results. Researcher illustration adapted from Avataaars (Pablo Stanley; Fang-Pen Lin). See Acknowledgments for artwork credits."
#| fig-alt: "Four-panel comic showing untreated and IFN-beta-stimulated samples from the same donors, with T cells, B cells and monocytes. Overlapping colored layers represent cell identity and stimulation effects on gene expression. CoGAPS infers patterns from an expression matrix. A researcher then examines contributing genes and compares cell activities to ask whether a response is shared. All grids, colors and patterns are schematic."
#| out-width: "900px"
#| out-extra: '.lightbox title=""'
ottrpal::include_slide(
```

Similar questions arise in other areas of research, where cells can share a biological response while retaining their distinct identities. CoGAPS has been used to investigate cell types and developmental processes in the mouse retina [@steinobrien2019transferLearning], to examine {{< glossary "Neural development" display="neural development" >}} [@kim2024neuralFates], and to examine immune-cell states associated with {{< glossary "Cancer immunotherapy" display="cancer immunotherapy" >}} [@davismarcisak2021nkActivation]. You can apply this approach in your own research to identify genes associated with each pattern and compare pattern activity across cell types and experimental conditions [@johnson2023cogapsWorkflow].

This case study uses data from Kang and colleagues [-@kang2018multiplexed], who studied how blood immune cells from eight people with SLE respond to IFN-beta. These {{< glossary "Peripheral blood mononuclear cell" display="peripheral blood mononuclear cells" >}} (PBMCs) include T cells, B cells, and monocytes. For each donor, the researchers exposed one portion of the cells to IFN-beta and left another untreated as a control, then measured RNA in individual cells six hours later. Comparing the two conditions helps us investigate whether different immune-cell types share a response to IFN-beta.

::::{.definition_box_header}
Motivating articles
::::
::::{.inner_block}

- **Source data: Kang et al. [-@kang2018multiplexed].** This study measured gene expression in individual blood immune cells from eight donors with SLE, comparing IFN-beta-stimulated samples with untreated samples from the same donors. We use these data to investigate shared and cell-type-associated responses.
- **Analysis method: Johnson et al. [-@johnson2023cogapsWorkflow].** This paper describes workflows for using CoGAPS to identify and interpret patterns in gene-expression data. It supports our analysis approach; CoGAPS was not used in the original Kang study.

::::
